lesson_title: Day 3 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 2 (Bitcoin transactions, wallets and multi-sig)

questions.question_stem: An unspent output pays to an address beginning with 3. What can an analyst correctly record about its spending rule?
questions.correct_answer: Only that it locks to a script hash; the actual rule, such as a 2-of-3 multisig, is revealed when it is spent.
incorrect_answers: That it is native SegWit, because the leading 3 marks the SegWit program in the way a bc1q prefix does.
That it is a single-key wallet, because only that kind of wallet uses a hash in its locking script here.
That it is a Taproot output, because Taproot hides its spending rule even after the output is later spent.
questions.explanation: A 3... output is P2SH: it commits to a script hash, and the redeem script appears only in the spending input. The 3 prefix alone does not mean SegWit (native SegWit is bc1q, Taproot is bc1p), and a 3... output can wrap a single-key SegWit wallet, so the prefix alone does not give the rule.

specific_source.reading: Script type says what kind of wallet paid

questions.question_stem: An explorer prints 23:11 UTC beside a payment. Which sentence in a trace is accurate?
questions.correct_answer: It was mined in a block with a miner-stated time of 23:11 UTC; block height, not time, sets the order.
incorrect_answers: It was sent at 23:11 UTC, because the transaction carries the timestamp that the sender's wallet wrote.
It was paid before its block, because the printed time is when the network first saw the transaction.
It was confirmed at 23:11 UTC, because block times rise on every block and so fix the exact order.
questions.explanation: A transaction has no timestamp of its own; the explorer shows the block's time, which the miner wrote and which need not rise from block to block. Order of events comes from block height.

specific_source.reading: A transaction has no timestamp of its own

questions.question_stem: A transaction paid a very large fee. A colleague concludes a very large payment was made. What is the best correction?
questions.correct_answer: The fee shows how much block space was bought and how urgently, in sat/vB; it does not show the amount sent.
incorrect_answers: The fee is a fixed share of the amount sent, so only a transaction that paid a small fee moved little value overall.
The fee is set by the receiver's wallet type, so it shows which address kind was paid and little else.
The fee goes back to the sender's old addresses, so a large one shows how many inputs the wallet merged.
questions.explanation: Miners rank waiting transactions by fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte. A fee shows the space bought and the urgency, not how much was sent. The wallet chooses the rate, so a repeated rate is only behavior.

specific_source.reading: Fees are priced per virtual byte, not per BTC

questions.question_stem: A lightweight wallet receives a short list of hashes for a payment and rebuilds the block header's Merkle root from them. What has it established?
questions.correct_answer: That the payment is included in that block; it says nothing about who sent it or owns it.
incorrect_answers: That the sender controls all the inputs, because the rebuilt root signs for each one of them.
That it is the only payment in its block, since a single path of hashes covers one leaf alone.
That every other transaction in the block is valid, because the root commits to all of them.
questions.explanation: A Merkle proof is the transaction's sibling hashes up to the root. If the rebuilt root matches the header, the transaction is in the block. Inclusion is not attribution, and the proof checks no other transaction's validity.

specific_source.reading: A Merkle proof shows a tx is in a block

questions.question_stem: A subject says deleting the wallet app from a phone destroyed the bitcoin it held. Which statement about where the coins are is correct?
questions.correct_answer: The coins remain as outputs on the blockchain; the wallet only stored the keys and addresses that control them.
incorrect_answers: The coins were stored inside the app, so deleting it removed them from the chain along with its data.
The coins sat in the phone's memory, so only a fresh app on that same phone can show them once more.
The coins were held by the app's maker, so the maker alone decides whether they ever come back to the user.
questions.explanation: The coins stay on the blockchain; a wallet is software holding the keys and addresses that control them. Deleting the app removes access only if no seed phrase or other key backup exists.

specific_source.reading: A wallet holds keys, not coins

questions.question_stem: Alice and Bob both have accounts at one exchange. Alice pays Bob inside the platform. What will an analyst find on chain?
questions.correct_answer: Possibly nothing; the exchange logs the transfer on its own books, so that evidence lies off chain.
incorrect_answers: A single transaction from Alice's deposit address to Bob's, since every customer transfer must be mined.
A transaction from Alice's own wallet to Bob's, since the exchange keeps no keys of its own to spend.
A pair of withdrawals and deposits, since each internal transfer is split into two matching entries.
questions.explanation: In a custodial wallet the platform holds the keys and records internal transfers on its own books, off-chain. A payment between two customers of one exchange may never reach the chain.

specific_source.reading: Whoever holds the key controls the coins

questions.question_stem: A large balance has not moved for two years. From the chain alone, how should the analyst characterize its storage?
questions.correct_answer: As possibly cold storage, stated with low confidence; a single transaction cannot show which device signed it.
incorrect_answers: As cold storage with high confidence, since only an offline hardware wallet can hold a balance for so long.
As custodial storage with high confidence, since only an exchange can leave a balance unspent for so long.
As a hot wallet with moderate confidence, since a transaction records the device that holds the signing key.
questions.explanation: A transaction carries scripts and signatures, not the signing device. Cold storage holds high-value funds at rest, so a long idle balance suggests it, but that is an inference from behavior: low confidence from the chain alone.

specific_source.reading: Hot or cold says where the key lives

questions.question_stem: An agent recovers a written 12-word seed phrase from one subject and an account xpub from another. How do the two differ for linking addresses?
questions.correct_answer: The phrase links every account and address type of the wallet and can spend; the xpub links one account.
incorrect_answers: The xpub links every account and address type and can spend; the phrase lists one account only.
Both link every account of the wallet equally, and both can spend, since each comes from the same one seed.
Neither links addresses at all, since the addresses from one seed cannot be tied together by anyone.
questions.explanation: A seed phrase is the whole wallet and links all accounts and address types. An account xpub derives that account's public keys, past and future, but no private key and nothing beyond hardened levels.

specific_source.reading: An xpub reveals every address, past and future

questions.question_stem: An explorer shows a native SegWit 2-of-3 spend with an empty item, two signatures and a witness script. Which report is supported?
questions.correct_answer: Two of three listed keys signed; who holds the keys, or how many people are involved, is not shown.
incorrect_answers: Two of the three signers approved it, so three named people hold the keys to this wallet together.
Two signatures prove two people took part, because each valid signature must come from a different one.
The first key belongs to the lead signer, since the script sets the keys out in rank order.
questions.explanation: The chain shows m, n, all n public keys and m valid signatures. It does not show who holds each key, or whether one person holds all three. Statements about people need separate evidence.

specific_source.reading: What a multi-sig spend shows, and what not

questions.question_stem: A draft says the first public key in a 2-of-3 script is the lead signer. Why is that wrong?
questions.correct_answer: Wallets usually sort the keys before building the script, so position is arithmetic and shows no roles.
incorrect_answers: Script requires the keys to be set out alphabetically by owner name, so position follows the owner's name.
Signatures may be given in any order, so the script never fixes which key is checked against which.
Only the last key in the script can sign, so the first one listed is the least likely to have signed.
questions.explanation: BIP 67 and the sortedmulti descriptor sort keys so the same set always gives the same address. Key position is therefore arithmetic, not hierarchy; write that order shows nothing about roles.

specific_source.reading: Key order in the script carries no meaning

questions.question_stem: A bc1p... output is spent by a key-path spend that shows a single signature. What can the analyst conclude about the number of signers?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing definite; a MuSig2 key-path spend looks like a single signer, so write what the spend shows.
incorrect_answers: That one person signed alone, because a multi-sig of any kind always shows its several keys on chain.
That a 2-of-3 multi-sig was used, because Taproot spends always reveal the threshold and the key count.
That the output was not a multi-sig, since the multi-sig script is absent from every Taproot spend.
questions.explanation: MuSig2 combines n keys into one, and its outputs are indistinguishable from single-signer Taproot outputs. Absence of a multi-sig script is not evidence of one signer; describe the spend type, not a signer count.

specific_source.reading: Taproot multi-sig can look like one key

questions.question_stem: A trace shows a multi-sig spend, and a prosecutor asks whether Electrum or Bitcoin Core built it. What does the chain itself offer?
questions.correct_answer: No program name is on chain; it shows the script type and the transaction that the program built.
incorrect_answers: The program name is stored in the witness next to the signatures, so the analyst only has to read it.
The program is named by the input's sequence field, so each of the three examples sets its own values.
The program shows in the fee field, where each wallet writes its own tag beside the amount it pays.
questions.explanation: The slide notes that none of these programs appears on chain by name: what you see is the script type and the transaction they built. Any inference about the program is a clue only.

specific_source.reading: Wallet software builds, signs and broadcasts
